name: @org/source
// typecheck: The root project has TypeScript files of its own — `vitest.config.ts` and `vitest.workspace.ts` — and until 2026-08-05 no compiler saw them, because they belong to neither a library nor an application. Same defect as `lesson-42`, one floor up: there a project went untypechecked, here the gap BETWEEN projects did. The configuration lives in `tsconfig.root.json`, not `tsconfig.json`: a file under the latter name at the root takes over the whole repository in the editor and in every tool that searches up the tree.
// check-typecheck: The typecheck gate walks the whole graph, so like `check-docs` it lives in the root project. `inputs` name EVERYTHING it reads: TypeScript files (the denominator), tsconfigs (the compiler programs) and `project.json`, `package.json`, `nx.json` (the graph, including targets inferred by plugins). The patterns are global because a new project has to be covered from its first commit — a hard-coded list would drift at the first new library, and the gate would be the one to stop seeing, not CI to fire.
// check-tokens: The token gate (names, tiers, pairs) lives in the root project rather than in `tokens`, and not for convenience: it reads package ENTRYPOINTS (`libs/components/*/ng-package.json`) and the library STYLESHEETS, while `tokens` is a dependency of `components` and not the other way round — so a change in the library does not make the tokens project affected. A removed entrypoint with `component.<name>.json` left behind would slip past the gate built partly for that. The root project is affected by every change (measured in A7), so this gate always runs. `dependsOn` on the tokens build is hard: the gate compares ARTIFACTS in `dist` against the DTCG sources and without them has nothing to compare. Stylesheets are in `inputs` since A12: point 7 asks what the library REALLY paints, so a new `background:` declaration has to invalidate this cache — otherwise the first unmeasured color would ride through on a cache hit.
// check-parts: The parts inventory gate lives in the root project for two reasons at once. First it reads `docs/components/*.md` — the **Parts** tables are the only surface where a consumer ever sees that inventory — and `docs/` belongs to no library, so a target in `components` would not move when only a card changes. Second, the root project is affected by EVERY change (measured in A7), and this gate guards the public styling API: the day it does not run is the day a part disappears without a trace. `dependsOn` on the library build is hard — the second reading of the inventory takes `ɵcmp` from the built package, not from sources, and without it has nothing to compare.
// check-browsers: The browser matrix gate lives in the root project although it is about `sandbox-e2e`, and not for convenience: it reads `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (point 5 — which engines the workflow installs and whether `e2e` is on the list at all), and a workflow belongs to no application. A target in `sandbox-e2e` would not move when only CI changes, leaving it blind to exactly the way of shrinking the matrix that leaves no trace in the Playwright configuration. The root project is affected by EVERY change (measured in A7), so the gate always runs. `inputs` name everything it reads: the e2e configuration and policy, the spec files (the denominator of point 3), the workflow and `project.json` (the `e2e` target is INFERRED by `@nx/playwright/plugin`, so its command comes from the graph, not from a file). No `dependsOn`: the measurement goes through `playwright test --list`, which starts neither a server nor a browser — and the probe in point 6 asks about engine behaviour, not about this library.
// check-docs: The documentation gate: every promise in docs/ names a gate and its reference control, and the named paths exist and run in CI. It lives in the root project because `docs/` belongs to no library — which is what makes a documentation change mark this project affected. The comment sits HERE rather than in `targets`: there a value must be a target object, and a string blows up the Nx graph (`lesson-43`).
